look_here_first: Introduced SILKY BLUESTEM (not a native Texas bluestem). Examine the silvery-hairy flowering head and narrow, often paired racemes, and then magnify the companion sterile/pedicelled spikelet against the awned sessile fertile spikelet. Compare the basal clump and hairy stem nodes against invasive Kleberg bluestem. This photo shows only one small silky head held against fingers, not definitive spikelet dissection.

best_field_traits: Often tufted perennial to about 1 m, sometimes with short rhizomes; annual/perennial treatments may differ by subspecies.
Culms can have hairy or bearded nodes and narrow linear-lanceolate leaf blades.
Many silky long hairs around spikelet pairs and axes yield pale, sometimes purple, fuzzy appearance.
Sessile fertile spikelet around 4 mm in Flora Zambesiaca treatment; awn twisted, bent, sometimes ~25 mm.
Texas occurrence introduced according to Kew; do not place into local-native dashboard metrics.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full flowering head with count of racemes against ruler
A mature spikelet pair; sterile companion glume hair vs fertile awn
Node hair sheath and stem; true collar ligule
Base to document tuft/rhizome not inferred from hand-held sample
crew_field_check: Start from whole rooted plant to establish growth form.
Photograph flowering head and collar on same individual.
Use hand-lens/25x macro to measure floret structure when needed; photos without it support only provisional source determination.
No county native certification; Kew states D. annulatum and D. sericeum are introduced in Texas.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) usually has more clearly 2–15 fingerlike racemes and prominently WHITE-RINGED stem nodes, sometimes a creeping/stoloniferous base. D. sericeum's densely silky hair and narrow racemes are useful orientation cues, NOT decisive alone; mature spikelet, paired sterile companion, node and root base necessary. Both species introduced in Texas.
